summary: Describes IBM's Shared Memory Communications over RDMA protocol. It provides RDMA communications to TCP endpoints in a way that is transparent to socket applications, with dynamic discovery of partner RDMA capabilities.

eli5.summary: Two computers use a fast direct memory path while programs still think they use normal networking.

subtitle: Let TCP applications use high-speed RDMA without knowing it

tldr.problem: TCP is reliable but slow because it involves the operating system and network stack; RDMA can be much faster but requires applications to know about it and breaks on complex networks.
tldr.mechanism: SMC-R intercepts TCP connections and transparently redirects their data over RDMA on Ethernet, while keeping TCP semantics intact and handling discovery, resilience, and fallback automatically.
tldr.outcome: Existing TCP applications get RDMA speed transparently, with automatic failover across redundant hardware and seamless fallback to IP if RDMA is unavailable.

today: RFC 7609 is an Informational RFC describing IBM's SMC-R protocol. It has not been obsoleted. SMC-R is deployed in production environments to accelerate enterprise data transfers and high-performance computing workloads while maintaining full compatibility with existing TCP applications and network infrastructure.

sections.title: Transparent RDMA for TCP
sections.content:
SMC-R (Shared Memory Communications over RDMA) enables RDMA communication between TCP socket endpoints without requiring application changes. It runs below the sockets layer and intercepts TCP connections, allowing data to be moved over RDMA instead of through the TCP stack when both peers support the protocol. The key innovation is that it is completely transparent: applications use normal TCP sockets and see no difference, yet data flows over a much faster RDMA path.

The protocol runs over RoCE (RDMA over Converged Ethernet), which allows RDMA semantics on standard Ethernet hardware with RDMA-capable NICs. SMC-R handles dynamic discovery of peer RDMA capabilities, automatic setup of RDMA connections, and transparent failover across redundant hardware. If RDMA setup fails at any point, the connection falls back to normal TCP over IP without disrupting the application.
sections.eli5: SMC-R is like having a smart traffic manager that detects when two drivers are heading to the same place and automatically gives them a faster route, but keeps the normal route ready in case something goes wrong.

sections.title: Links, Link Groups, and Memory Buffers
sections.content:
An SMC-R link is a logical point-to-point connection between two peers using RDMA queue pairs over the RoCE fabric. Each link is tied to specific network adapters (RNICs) and a VLAN if applicable. One SMC-R link can carry multiple TCP connections, multiplexed by the SMC-R layer.

SMC-R links are organized into link groups. When redundant hardware exists—for example, two RNICs on each peer—multiple SMC-R links within a link group provide load balancing and transparent failover. If one RNIC fails, existing TCP connections automatically switch to a surviving link in the group without application intervention. Each peer can create multiple Remote Memory Buffers (RMBs) in its local memory and share access to them via RDMA keys (RKeys) with the peer, allowing the peer to write data directly into the buffers using RDMA writes.
sections.eli5: A link is like a cable between two computers. A link group is like having multiple cables for redundancy. Memory buffers are like mailboxes that each computer lets the other computer write into directly.

sections.title: Negotiation and Setup
sections.content:
When a TCP connection begins, a rendezvous protocol runs during and after the three-way handshake. The TCP client and server first signal SMC-R capability using a new TCP option. If both peers are capable, they exchange Connection Layer Control (CLC) messages over the TCP connection to negotiate RDMA credentials: which queue pair to use, the VLAN ID if needed, and the RKeys and addresses for accessing each other's RMBs.

If both peers agree, one SMC-R link is either reused (for subsequent connections) or created (for first contact). The peers also exchange RMB information via Link Layer Control (LLC) messages sent over the RDMA fabric itself. Once negotiation completes successfully, the SMC-R layers hand the sockets back to the application, and all TCP data flows over RDMA out-of-band, leaving the TCP connection open but idle except for keepalive or teardown traffic. If negotiation fails at any point, the connection continues using normal TCP over IP.
sections.eli5: Two computers meet and say to each other: 'Hey, do you support the fast lane (RDMA)?' If both say yes, they exchange instructions on how to use it. If anything goes wrong, they just use the normal road.

sections.title: Data Transfer via Shared Buffers
sections.content:
Each TCP connection is allocated an RMB Element (RMBE) from a shared RMB—a fixed-size buffer that represents the TCP receive buffer. When the sender writes data into the receiver's RMBE using RDMA, it also sends a Connection Data Control (CDC) message that tells the receiver the write is complete. The CDC message includes control flags (such as urgent data markers) and two cursors: a producer cursor (how much data the sender has written) and a consumer cursor (how much space is available for writes).

The receiver reads the data from its local RMBE and sends a CDC message back to update its consumer cursor, telling the sender how much space is now available. This coordinated cursor-based flow control prevents buffer overflow while minimizing the number of control messages. The architecture allows multiple RMBs per link with different buffer sizes, enabling efficient resource sharing across many TCP connections between the same peers.
sections.eli5: Two neighbors share a mailbox. One neighbor writes a letter and rings the doorbell to say 'there's a letter at position 50'. The other neighbor reads it and says 'I read up to position 50, so you can write more after that'. They coordinate without confusion.

sections.title: High Availability and Failover
sections.content:
When redundant RNICs are present on both peers, symmetric link groups provide both load balancing and failure protection. TCP connections can be distributed across multiple links, increasing aggregate bandwidth. If an RNIC fails, the SMC-R layer transparently moves affected connections to a surviving link in the link group by using the existing TCP connection state and coordinated RMBE cursors.

The architecture supports up to eight symmetric links in a single link group, with a minimum of two links required for redundancy. This allows operators to add a third link before removing an old one, supporting graceful maintenance. TCP keepalive flows help detect link failures, and Connection Data Control messages maintain visibility into data that has been transferred, enabling safe resumption on a new path. If no redundant link is available, the connection can be resumed over normal TCP/IP.
sections.eli5: If one of the four cables between two buildings gets cut, traffic automatically switches to the remaining three cables. The delivery service never stops.

sections.title: Implementation and Scope
sections.content:
The specification recommends that SMC-R be implemented in kernel space, where it can share resources across multiple processes and survive process forking. User-space implementations are compatible with the architecture but are limited to resource sharing within a single process. The protocol does not require a separate RDMA connection manager; peer discovery and setup are embedded in the rendezvous handshake using TCP itself.

SMC-R preserves TCP semantics and qualities of service: filtering rules remain effective, SSL/TLS encryption works transparently, TCP urgent data is supported, and the three-way handshake is maintained. The hardware requirements are modest: standard Ethernet switches with IEEE 802.3x Global Pause Frame support and RDMA-capable NICs. While designed for RoCE, the rendezvous methods could be adapted to other RDMA fabrics such as InfiniBand or iWARP.
sections.eli5: SMC-R is best built into the operating system kernel so it can help all programs, but it can also run as a user program if needed. It fits into the existing network security and encryption mechanisms.
